addedLines: - claude: Catch-all for any task that doesn't fit a more specific agent. FleetView's default when no agent name is typed. (Tools: *)

- Explore: Read-only search agent for broad fan-out searches — when answering means sweeping many files, directories, or naming conventions and you only need the conclusion, not the file dumps. It reads excerpts rather than whole files, so it locates code; it doesn't review or audit it. Specify search breadth: "medium" for moderate exploration, "very thorough" for multiple locations and naming conventions. (Tools: All tools except Agent, Artifact, ExitPlanMode, Edit, Write, NotebookEdit)

- general-purpose: General-purpose agent for researching complex questions, searching for code, and executing multi-step tasks. When you are searching for a keyword or file and are not confident that you will find the right match in the first few tries use this agent to perform the search for you. (Tools: *)

- Plan: Software architect agent for designing implementation plans. Use this when you need to plan the implementation strategy for a task. Returns step-by-step plans, identifies critical files, and considers architectural trade-offs. (Tools: All tools except Agent, Artifact, ExitPlanMode, Edit, Write, NotebookEdit)
- statusline-setup: Use this agent to configure the user's Claude Code status line setting. (Tools: Read, Edit)

attachment.content:
- agent-browser: Browser automation CLI for AI agents. Use when the user needs to interact with websites, including navigating pages, filling forms, clicking buttons, taking screenshots, extracting data, testing web apps, or automating any browser task. Triggers include requests to "open a website", "fill out a form", "click a button", "take a screenshot", "scrape data from a page", "test this web app", "login to a site", "automate browser actions", or any task requiring programmatic web interaction. Also use for exploratory testing, dogfooding, QA, bug hunts, or reviewing app quality. Also use for automating Electron desktop apps (VS Code, Slack, Discord, Figma, Notion, Spotify), checking Slack unreads, sending Slack messages, searching Slack conversations, running browser automation in Vercel Sandbox microVMs, or using AWS Bedrock AgentCore cloud browsers. Prefer agent-browser over any built-in browser automation or web tools.
- portless: Set up and use portless for named local dev server URLs (e.g. https://myapp.localhost instead of http://localhost:3000). Use when integrating portless into a project, configuring dev server names, setting up the local proxy, working with .localhost domains, or troubleshooting port/proxy issues.
- unslop: Cut AI tells from any writing. Must always apply.
- video-use: Edit any video by conversation. Transcribe, cut, color grade, generate overlay animations, burn subtitles — for talking heads, montages, tutorials, travel, interviews. No presets, no menus. Ask questions, confirm the plan, execute, iterate, persist. Production-correctness rules are hard; everything else is artistic freedom.
- frontend-design:frontend-design: Guidance for distinctive, intentional visual design when building new UI or reshaping an existing one. Helps with aesthetic direction, typography, and making choices that don't read as templated defaults.
- dataviz: Use this skill whenever you are about to create ANY chart, graph, plot, dashboard, or data visualization, in ANY output medium — an HTML or React artifact, inline SVG, plotting code in any library (matplotlib, plotly, d3, Recharts, …), an image/PNG you will render and upload, or a chart shared into Slack. Read it BEFORE writing the first line of chart code, choosing chart colors, building a stat tile / meter / KPI row, or laying out a dashboard. Produces visualizations that read as one system — elegant, accessible, consistent in light and dark — using a brand-neutral placeholder palette you swap for your own. Teaches a design-system-agnostic method: a form heuristic, a color formula with a runnable validator, mark specs, and interaction rules. A validated default palette is documented in `references/palette.md` — swap that file's values for your brand's. Triggers on: "chart", "graph", "plot", "data viz", "visualization", "dashboard", "analytics", "visualize data", "categorical colors", "sequential / diverging palette", "stat tile", "sparkline", "heatmap", "legend", "axis", "tooltip", "chart colors", "color by series".
- update-config: Use this skill to configure the Claude Code harness via settings.json. Automated behaviors ("from now on when X", "each time X", "whenever X", "before/after X") require hooks configured in settings.json - the harness executes these, not Claude, so memory/preferences cannot fulfill them. Also use for: permissions ("allow X", "add permission", "move permission to"), env vars ("set X=Y"), hook troubleshooting, or any changes to settings.json/settings.local.json files. Examples: "allow npm commands", "add bq permission to global settings", "move permission to user settings", "set DEBUG=true", "when claude stops show X". For simple settings like theme/model, suggest the /config command.
- keybindings-help: Use when the user wants to customize keyboard shortcuts, rebind keys, add chord bindings, or modify ~/.claude/keybindings.json. Examples: "rebind ctrl+s", "add a chord shortcut", "change the submit key", "customize keybindings".
- code-review: Review the current diff, or a PR number/branch/path target, for correctness bugs and reuse/simplification/efficiency cleanups at the given effort level (low/medium: fewer, high-confidence findings; high→max: broader coverage, may include uncertain findings; ultra: deep multi-agent review in the cloud); with no level given, it reuses the level you typed last. Pass --comment to post findings as inline PR comments, or --fix to apply the findings to the working tree after the review. For ultra on a GitHub.com PR target, --post asks to post the finished review’s findings to the PR as a single comment from the user’s GitHub account (not a review; the launch dialog still confirms in interactive sessions, while non-interactive mode posts on the flag alone) and --no-post hides that option.
- simplify: Review the changed code for reuse, simplification, efficiency, and altitude cleanups, then apply the fixes. Quality only — it does not hunt for bugs; use /code-review for that.
- fewer-permission-prompts: Scan your transcripts for common read-only Bash and MCP tool calls, then add a prioritized allowlist to project .claude/settings.json to reduce permission prompts.
- loop: Run a prompt or slash command on a recurring interval (e.g. /loop 5m /foo). Omit the interval to let the model self-pace. - When the user wants to set up a recurring task, poll for status, or run something repeatedly on an interval (e.g. "check the deploy every 5 minutes", "keep running /babysit-prs"). Do NOT invoke for one-off tasks.
- schedule: Create, update, list, or run scheduled cloud agents (routines) that execute on a cron schedule. - When the user wants to schedule a recurring cloud agent, set up automated tasks, create a cron job for Claude Code, or manage their scheduled agents/routines. Also use when the user wants a one-time scheduled run ("run this once at 3pm", "remind me to check X tomorrow").
- claude-api: Reference for the Claude API / Anthropic SDK — model ids, pricing, params, streaming, tool use, MCP, agents, caching, token counting, model migration.
TRIGGER — read BEFORE opening the target file; don't skip because it "looks like a one-liner" — whenever: the prompt names Claude/Anthropic in any form (Claude, Anthropic, Fable, Opus, Sonnet, Haiku, `anthropic`, `@anthropic-ai`, `claude-*`, `us.anthropic.*`, `[1m]`); the user asks about an LLM (pricing/model choice/limits/caching) — never answer from memory; OR the task is LLM-shaped with provider unstated (agent/MCP/tool-definition/multi-agent/RAG/LLM-judge/computer-use; generate/summarize/extract/classify/rewrite/converse over NL; debugging refusals/cutoffs/streaming/tool-calls/tokens).
SKIP only when another provider is being worked on (overrides all triggers): OpenAI/GPT/Gemini/Llama/Mistral/Cohere/Ollama named in the query; OR `grep -rE 'openai|langchain_openai|google.generativeai|genai|mistralai|cohere|ollama'` over the project hits (run this grep FIRST if no provider named — don't Read the file).
- run: Launch and drive this project's app to see a change working. Use when asked to run, start, or screenshot the app, or to confirm a change works in the real app (not just tests). First looks for a project skill that already covers launching the app; otherwise falls back to built-in patterns per project type (CLI, server, TUI, Electron, browser-driven, library).
- init: Initialize a new CLAUDE.md file with codebase documentation
- security-review: Complete a security review of the pending changes on the current branch

# mikrotik

## Запуск локально

1. Установка Go:

    Для начала установите Go на свой компьютер, следуя инструкциям на официальном сайте: Установка Go
    Клонирование репозитория:

    Clone with HTTPS:
    git clone https://gitlab.wildberries.ru/pmg/pmg/mikrotik.git

    Clone with SSH:
    git clone git@gitlab.wildberries.ru:pmg/pmg/mikrotik.git

2. Использование Go модулей:

    Установить зависимости:
    go mod tidy

    Если в процессе установки зависимостей вы столкнулись с ошибкой
    "fatal: could not read Username for : terminal prompts disabled",
     просьба рассмотреть следующие шаги для ее устранения:

        1. Добавьте GOPRIVATE

        GOPRIVATE='gitlab.wildberries.ru/*'
        export GOPRIVATE

        2. Убедитесь, что в GIT CONFIG У ВАС УСТАНОВЛЕН USER.NAME, USER.EMAIL, URL.GIT@

        git config --global user.name "YOUR_USERNAME"
        git config --global user.email "YOUR_EMAIL"
        git config --global url."git@gitlab.wildberries.ru:wbx-index/platform/scratch".insteadof https://gitlab.wildberries.ru/wbx-index/platform/scratch

        Для просмотра git config можно использовать команду
        git config --list
        или
        cat ~/.gitconfig

        после чего попробуйте еще раз установить зависимости
        go mod tidy

Based on the search results, here's the documentation for the frp bandwidth limiting feature for per-proxy configuration:

## Bandwidth Limiting Configuration

To enable bandwidth limiting per proxy, add the `transport.bandwidthLimit` field to the proxy configuration. Currently only MB and KB units are supported.

## Bandwidth Limit Mode

Rate limiting is implemented on the client side by default. If you want to enable server-side rate limiting, you need to additionally configure `transport.bandwidthLimitMode = "server"`. Valid values include "client" and "server", with "client" being the default.

## Example Configuration

An example proxy configuration would look like: `transport.bandwidthLimit = "10MB"` and `transport.bandwidthLimitMode = "server"`.

This allows you to control the bandwidth for each proxy individually, choosing whether the rate limiting should be enforced on the client side (frpc) or server side (frps).

content.text:
I cloned frp (`758f07d`, Aug 18 2026) and read both implementations. Short answer: **no, they're solving different problems.** frp does a plain in-process token bucket; this repo does two-level distributed pacing. Neither is "better" in the abstract, but each has concrete weaknesses.

## How frp limits traffic

Everything lives in `pkg/util/limit/` — about 120 lines total.

**The limiter** (`limiter.go:25`): `rate.NewLimiter(rate.Limit(bytes), burst=bytes)` from `golang.org/x/time/rate`. A standard token bucket where **burst equals one full second** of the configured rate, not tunable.

**Application** (`reader.go`, `writer.go`): thin `io.Reader`/`io.Writer` wrappers. Reader clamps the buffer to burst, reads, then calls `limiter.WaitN(context.Background(), n)`. Writer chunks the payload to burst size and waits *before* each write.

**Scope**: one limiter per *proxy*, built once in `NewProxy` (`server/proxy/proxy.go:536`, `client/proxy/proxy.go:66`) and stored on `BaseProxy`. All work connections of that proxy share it.

Four things fall out of that design that matter:

1. **Reader and Writer get the same limiter object** (`server/proxy/proxy.go:311`, `client/proxy/proxy.go:137`). Upload and download draw from one combined budget — a saturated download starves the upload.
2. **The limiter is never updated.** There's no `SetLimiter`; changing a limit requires recreating the proxy.
3. **`context.Background()` in `WaitN`** means a throttle wait isn't cancellable by connection close or shutdown.
4. **Layering is asymmetric.** Client-side the limiter wraps the raw conn (below encryption/compression, so it counts *wire* bytes); server-side it wraps outermost (so it counts *plaintext, uncompressed* bytes). With `useCompression = true`, `bandwidthLimitMode = "client"` and `"server"` meter different quantities.

Mode is `client` (default) or `server` (`pkg/config/types/types.go:29`). Client mode puts enforcement on the untrusted end — a patched frpc just doesn't limit. Server-side plugins can mutate `BandwidthLimit` at proxy registration (`pkg/plugin/server/manager.go:133`), so central *policy* is possible, but enforcement stays a local bucket in one process.

## How this repo limits traffic

Two levels, in `internal/modules/bandwidth/pacer.go` and `internal/adapters/redislimiter/scheduler.go`.

**Global**: GCRA in a Redis Lua script. The key holds a theoretical arrival time in µs of Redis server time; each reservation advances it by `bytes/rate` and returns `TAT - now - burst_tolerance` as the required delay. The key embeds rate and burst (`scheduler.go:104`) so a limits change starts a fresh schedule.

**Local**: `Pacer` keeps a per-`(route, direction)` lease and only calls Redis when the lease runs dry, reserving `DefaultLeaseBytes` = 512 KiB at a time. The clever part is `refreshGrant` (`pacer.go:167`): it folds the global delay into the local TAT so many concurrent connections on one instance interleave against a single local schedule instead of all sleeping the same delay.

Traffic is chunked at 32 KiB (`stream.go:19`), so one Redis round trip amortizes over ~16 chunks. Limits are per-direction, burst is configurable (default 64 KiB), waits are ctx-cancellable, and limits hot-swap through `atomic.Pointer[RateLimits]` with `Registry.Apply` preserving the pointer so in-flight transfers pick up new limits on the next chunk.

## Side by side

| | frp | this repo |
|---|---|---|
| Algorithm | Token bucket (`x/time/rate`) | GCRA, Redis + local |
| Scope of enforcement | One process | All instances (6 prod clusters) |
| Direction | Up+down share one budget | Separate per direction |
| Burst | Fixed at 1s of rate | Configurable, 64 KiB default |
| Live limit changes | No, requires proxy recreate | Yes, atomic swap mid-stream |
| Cancellable waits | No (`context.Background()`) | Yes (ctx + timer) |
| Data-path dependency | None | Redis, every 512 KiB |
| Failure mode | Can't fail | Redis error → `errThrottle` → conn dies |
| Observability | Traffic counters only | Traffic + throttle-wait histogram + outcomes |

## Which is better

**For frp's problem, frp's approach is right and this repo's would be wrong.** frp is a single-binary tunnel with no infrastructure assumptions. Putting Redis in its data path would be absurd. Its limiter is exact within the process, costs nothing, and has no failure mode.

**For this repo's problem, frp's approach doesn't work at all.** `.gitlab-ci.yml` deploys to six prod clusters. Six independent token buckets against shared MikroTik SOCKS5 upstreams means the effective limit is 6× the configured one. Redis coordination isn't gold-plating here, it's the requirement.

That said, two real weaknesses in the current design:

**Lease waste is the big one.** `refreshGrant` advances the *global* TAT by the full 512 KiB whether or not those bytes are ever sent. An instance that grabs a lease and then goes idle has burned that slice of the global schedule permanently — there's no lease return or expiry-based reclaim. Worst case is 6 × 512 KiB = 3 MiB of phantom reservation per route/direction. At the 2 Mbit/s default (250 KB/s), that's ~12 seconds of schedule spent on traffic that never happened. The remedy is either shrinking `DefaultLeaseBytes`, or sizing the lease adaptively from observed throughput so slow routes lease small and fast routes lease big.

**Fail-closed on Redis.** `Reserve` errors propagate as `errThrottle` and kill the connection (`stream.go:39`). Redis becomes a hard availability dependency for all proxy traffic. A local-only fallback — pace against the route limit alone, accept temporary N× overshoot, emit a metric — would trade exactness for survivability. Whether that's the right trade depends on whether the MikroTik caps are contractual or just protective; that's your call, but the choice should be deliberate rather than incidental.

**Worth borrowing from frp:** nothing structural. Its `limit.Reader`/`limit.Writer` are composable in a way the bespoke copy loop isn't, but `pacedReadCloser` already covers that ground. Its `context.Background()` and shared up/down budget are things this repo already got right.

Sources: [fatedier/frp](https://github.com/fatedier/frp), [frp bandwidth limit docs](https://gofrp.org/en/docs/reference/proxy/), [x/time/rate](https://pkg.go.dev/golang.org/x/time/rate)
